lessons.title: Gold: The Crisis Hedge With Long Flat Stretches

children.text: Ask two Indians about gold and you will get two opposite stories. One says gold saved the family in 2008 and again in 2020, when everything else was falling. The other says they bought gold for a wedding in 2012 and it went nowhere for the next seven years, while the Nifty doubled. Both are telling the truth. Gold is the one traditional asset that has genuinely protected Indian portfolios in crises, and it has also delivered some of the longest flat stretches of any asset you could own. This lesson measures both sides, so you know what gold's return and risk really look like before comparing it with anything alternative.

body.text: Gold is insurance that sometimes pays like an investment. It has no cash flows, long periods of going nowhere and moves driven by global fear and the rupee, which is exactly why it has held up when Indian equities have not.

children.text: The chart shows a staircase with a long landing in the middle. Gold rose steeply from 2005 to 2012, went nowhere until 2019, then climbed hard again. It kept rising sharply through 2025 to fresh record highs. Just like the Nifty, the return you got depended heavily on when you started.

children.text: The Flat Stretch: Seven Years of Waiting

stats.label: Gold in USD, 2011 peak to 2015 low

children.text: Globally, gold fell about 45% from its 2011 peak and did not get back there until 2020, nine years later. Indian investors had it easier, and the reason is the rupee.
Why Gold in Rupees Behaves Differently: The Currency Cushion

Gold is priced globally in US dollars. India imports nearly all of its gold, so the price you pay in Mumbai or Chennai is roughly the dollar price converted into rupees, plus import duty and GST. When the rupee weakens against the dollar, gold becomes more expensive in rupees even if the global price has not moved.

body.caption: R_INR = gold return in rupees, R_USD = gold return in dollars, D = rupee depreciation against the dollar

children.text: If global gold rises 5% in a year and the rupee weakens 3%, gold in rupees rises 1.05 × 1.03 − 1, or about 8.15%. The rupee has weakened by roughly 3 to 4% a year over the long run, which has quietly added to gold's rupee returns and softened its global falls. It is also why gold tends to shine in Indian crises: those are often the moments when the rupee drops sharply.

body.title: Gold, dollars and the rupee
body.prompt: In a particular year, the global gold price in dollars rises 10% and the rupee depreciates 4% against the dollar. Ignoring changes in duty and taxes, what is the return on gold in rupees, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 1.10 × 1.04 − 1 = 0.144, or 14.4%. The rupee's fall added more than 4 points on top of gold's global rise. The same effect works in reverse: in a year when the rupee strengthens, rupee gold returns lag global gold.

body.text: Gold is not a perfect hedge in the first days of a panic. In March 2020 it fell briefly alongside equities as investors sold whatever they could. Its protection shows up over months, not minutes, which is still far more useful than an appraised asset whose losses simply have not been recorded yet.

children.text: That is the trade: give up a point or two in normal years to take several points off the worst year. This is gold's real job in a portfolio, and it is the job many alternatives claim to do without having the crisis record to prove it.
What Drives Gold, and What It Cannot Do

columns.label: What gold does well
points: Has tended to rise in global and Indian crises
Near-zero long-run correlation with Indian equities
No credit risk: no borrower can default on it
Easy to hold and sell through gold ETFs on NSE

columns.label: What gold cannot do
points: Produce any income, rent, interest or dividends
Grow with India's economy or company earnings
Avoid long flat or falling stretches, like 2012 to 2019
Escape swings of roughly 12 to 16% a year in volatility
Be valued from cash flows, so there is no "fair price" to anchor to

markDefs.definition: An asset whose only return is a change in its price, because it produces no income such as rent, interest or dividends.

children.text: . Its price moves with global fear, the US dollar, real interest rates, and heavy buying by central banks, which has been a major force in recent years. Chapter 4 looks at other assets with no cash flows, such as commodities, collectibles and crypto. Gold is the most established member of that family, with centuries of history as money, which is a big part of why it has held its crisis role.

body.title: Key moments for gold in India

events.title: Balance of payments crisis
events.description: With foreign exchange reserves nearly exhausted, India pledged gold to raise emergency funds, cementing gold's image as the asset of last resort.

events.title: Global gold peaks
events.description: Gold hits about $1,920 an ounce, then begins a four-year global slide of roughly 45%.

events.title: Taper tantrum and import curbs
events.description: The rupee falls sharply, pushing rupee gold prices up even as global gold weakens. The government raises gold import duty to 10% to curb imports.

events.title: Sovereign Gold Bonds launched
events.description: The government offers paper gold with 2.5% interest to reduce physical gold imports.

events.title: Covid rally
events.description: Gold hits record highs globally and in India as rates are slashed and uncertainty spikes.

events.title: Duty cut
events.description: The Union Budget cuts the effective customs duty on gold from 15% to 6%, lowering domestic prices relative to global prices.

events.title: Fresh record highs
events.description: Heavy central bank buying and global uncertainty push gold to new records in dollars and rupees.

body.title: Gold's real role
body.question: Which statement best describes gold's risk-return profile for an Indian investor?
options: A steady compounder that beats equities in most seven-year periods
A risk-free asset, since it cannot default
A non-yielding asset with long flat stretches that has tended to hold up when Indian equities fall
An asset that moves in lockstep with the Nifty 50
body.explanation: Gold has no credit risk, but it is not risk-free: its price swings meaningfully and it went nowhere in rupees from 2012 to 2019. Its value lies in low correlation with equities and a solid crisis record, not in steady compounding.

body.title: What gold lacks
body.textWithBlank: Unlike shares, bonds or rental property, gold produces no ___, so its entire return comes from price changes.
body.explanation: Because gold pays no income, there is no cash flow to value it on. Its price depends entirely on what the next buyer will pay, which is why it can stay flat for years.

body.title: The Srinivasan family's gold
body.scenario: The Srinivasans in Madurai have about ₹1.5 crore in total wealth. Of that, ₹60 lakh is gold jewellery collected over 30 years, ₹50 lakh is their home, ₹25 lakh is in FDs and ₹15 lakh is in equity mutual funds. Their son, who works in Bengaluru, says: "Gold is 40% of our wealth. It always goes up. We should buy more."
body.prompt: Assess the family's gold holding using what you learned. Is 40% sensible, and is "it always goes up" true?
body.modelAnswer:
1. "It always goes up" is false. Gold in rupees was roughly flat from 2012 to 2019, and globally it fell about 45% between 2011 and 2015. Recent strong years do not guarantee the next seven.

2. 40% of total wealth, and about 60% of their investable wealth if the home is excluded (₹60 lakh of ₹1 crore), is far above the 5 to 15% often suggested for gold's hedging role. The family is heavily exposed to one non-yielding asset.

3. Jewellery is the least efficient form. Making charges have already been lost, and resale involves deductions, so its investment value is below its gold content's market price.

4. What gold does well still matters: it has protected Indian families in crises and carries no credit risk, so some gold is reasonable.

5. A more balanced approach: keep the jewellery they value for family and cultural reasons, but treat it as their gold allocation and do not add more. Direct new savings towards equity funds for growth and high-quality fixed income for stability. If they want more gold exposure in future, gold ETFs are cheaper and easier to sell than jewellery.

points: Gold in rupees has delivered roughly 12% a year since 2000, but only about 7.4% a year for someone who bought in 2012.
It can go nowhere for years: rupee gold barely moved from 2012 to 2019, while globally it fell about 45% between 2011 and 2015.
Rupee returns are roughly global gold returns plus rupee depreciation, which has cushioned Indian investors and boosted gold in local crises.
Gold has tended to rise in stress years like 2008, 2011 and 2020, and a 10 to 20% allocation can take several points off a severe crash year.
It produces no income, so its price rests on fear, the dollar, real interest rates and central bank buying rather than cash flows.
Judge any alternative that claims to be a crisis hedge against gold's long, public record, including its flat stretches.
